intro: Ives’s portrait of the Alcotts combines hymn-like chords with the rhythm of Beethoven’s Fifth, sometimes setting the piano’s hands in different keys. What lets you recognise a melody when its surroundings disagree?
question: How does a familiar rhythm survive clashing harmonies?

sections.label: Competing harmonies
sections.mNote: Beethoven-derived rhythm persists within thickened, conflicting harmonies

sections.label: The theme in C major
sections.mNote: complete human-faith melody assembled in broad C-major chords

relations.label: The parlour melody returns
relations.basis: The paired spans lie in the middle parlour-music episode, whose melodic paragraph recurs. Kyle Gann describes its two turns towards Wagner’s wedding tune at https://charlesives.org/node/6616; this link concerns the longer paragraph, not an individually timed quotation. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 29 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 40.5 s (cache/form/ives-concord-alcotts.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A hymn at home
cues.text: The opening presents the sonata’s recurring “human faith” melody in a comparatively direct, chordal setting. Listen for the shape of the tune across the spaces between chords, rather than expecting an unbroken stream of notes.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann’s Ives Society guide identifies the melody in this opening; the analysis shows relatively sparse piano attacks.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Three members of one family
cues.text: Ives’s accompanying essay discusses Bronson Alcott, the philosopher; Louisa May, the novelist; and Elizabeth, the family pianist who was the model for Beth in Little Women. The portrait includes domestic music-making as well as philosophical discussion.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann’s guide identifies these three figures from Ives’s Essays Before a Sonata.

cues.title: Beethoven inside Ives’s melody
cues.text: Across the stronger chordal passages, listen for the short-short-short-long rhythm associated with Beethoven’s Fifth. Ives incorporates that pattern into his own recurring melody; it can remain recognisable even when the surrounding harmony becomes crowded.
cues.evidence: Gann identifies Beethoven-derived material in these climaxes; the analysis places a broad increase in level around 1:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Following rhythm through dissonance
cues.text: The first large climax thickens the chordal sound. Try following the repeated-note rhythm through the conflicting harmonies: a rhythmic identity can remain clear even when a chord does not settle into one simple key.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the Beethoven-based climax; the recording’s strongest five-second window is around 1:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Music after the office
cues.text: Ives studied with Horatio Parker at Yale, then entered the New York insurance business in 1898. He remained a church organist until 1902; his later partnership with Julian Myrick supported a composing life outside the concert profession.
cues.evidence: Jan Swafford’s Ives Society biography documents Parker, the insurance career, the organ posts and the Myrick partnership.

cues.title: The parlour episode
cues.text: The middle episode borrows the manner of nineteenth-century parlour music: a singable tune with accompaniment rather than the earlier collisions of heavy chords. Compare the separation of melody and background with the opening.
cues.evidence: Gann identifies the parlour-music episode; a quieter interval before renewed activity near 3:00 supports its approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Printed for strangers
cues.text: Ives paid to print the sonata in 1920 and mailed copies to two hundred people in January 1921. John Kirkpatrick gave its complete public premiere at New York’s Town Hall on 20 January 1939, after earlier performances of individual movements.
cues.evidence: Gann’s Ives Society timeline records the printing, mailing and Kirkpatrick’s public premiere.

cues.title: Towards the final statement
cues.text: The later transition makes the familiar melodic manner less settled before the broad concluding statement. Listen for continuity of shape through the increasingly chromatic notes, rather than treating dissonance as a complete break with the tune.
cues.evidence: Gann describes a harmonically ambiguous transition; the analysis shows increased activity around 4:25–4:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The theme assembled
cues.text: The concluding statement gives the “human faith” melody in broad C major chords. In the complete sonata, material heard in fragments in “Emerson” and “Hawthorne” becomes a continuous tune; the Beethoven rhythm belongs within it.
cues.evidence: Gann identifies the final complete statement and its key; the audio change around 4:48 supplies an approximate location, not a score alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano’s remaining resonance
cues.text: The ending briefly recalls B♭ before its final C major chord. Listen through the remaining resonance as well as the last attack: the piano’s decay lengthens the close without adding more notes.
cues.evidence: Gann describes the closing harmonies; the analysis detects no further attacks in the final windows around 5:40–5:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Heavy chords become domestic accompaniment
transitions.how: After the Beethoven-based climax, the “human faith” melody has already returned quietly; Ives lets that chordal paragraph subside before introducing the parlour tune. The hands now separate into a singable upper line and accompaniment, rather than piling incompatible harmonic claims into the same attack. B♭ remains a point of reference, but the new melody’s Scottish-song turns and lighter articulation change the kind of music being made. This is a textural reset, not a classical development that must first reach a dominant pedal.
transitions.evidence: The map places the episode at 178 s, matching the 2:58 analysis boundary after the quiet 2:45–2:55 span. The form relation begins at 177 s. Kyle Gann’s score guide describes the quiet restatement before the parlour episode and its Scottish-song idiom: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: The parlour tune loses its bearings
transitions.how: Ives does not discard the parlour melody when its B♭-centred setting becomes unstable. He transforms its familiar turns through chromatic notes and increasingly crowded chords, while the piano’s attacks grow more insistent. Melody and bass no longer provide the easy agreement of tune and accompaniment. The passage is a link: recognisable shapes survive, but their harmonic destination is withheld until the broad C-major statement that follows.
transitions.evidence: The section boundary at 262 s is also the report’s strongest 4:22 boundary. Attacks and relative level increase through 4:25–4:40. Gann identifies this as a harmonically ambiguous transition that gradually transforms the Scottish-song idiom, not a securely named succession of local keys: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: The hands agree on C major
transitions.how: The chromatic link gives way to a complete statement of the “human faith” melody in broad C-major chords. The change is from competing or ambiguous harmony to agreement between the tune and its bass support, not simply from quiet to loud: the preceding passage has already accumulated force. The opening do–re–mi and the repeated-note Beethoven rhythm now belong to one continuous melody. Spacious chordal attacks replace the crowded transition and let the theme’s full span become audible.
transitions.evidence: The theme is mapped at 288 s, matching the analysis boundary at 4:48. Attack density drops after the 4:40 build, and C-major estimates become clearer at 4:50. Gann identifies the complete C-major statement and its Beethoven-derived component; the relations file does not claim a measured opening-to-ending match: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

transitions.title: B♭ interrupts the final certainty
transitions.how: The C-major statement recedes, but Ives briefly restores B♭ before the last C-major chord. That whole-tone displacement recalls the earlier tonal world without reopening the movement’s full argument. The bass and chordal texture carry the change; there is no run or conventional dominant bridge smoothing B♭ into C. As the spacing widens and the attacks lose force, the final C-major triad supplies a plain ending after the momentary harmonic backward glance.
transitions.evidence: Close begins at 330 s, the report’s 5:30 boundary, after a level drop at 5:25. B♭-centred estimates at 5:30–5:35 agree with Gann’s description of B♭ recalled before the final C-major chord. The final harmony comes from that score account, not the unreliable decay-window estimates: https://charlesives.org/node/6616 .

facts: With his father George Ives in Danbury; composition with Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; New York insurance business, ultimately Ives & Myrick
The Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata at his own expense; 114 Songs, 1922
American hymn tunes · marches · ragtime · Beethoven · Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
Charles Ives grew up in Danbury, Connecticut, where his father George directed bands, played the cornet and taught music. George had served as a Union bandmaster during the American Civil War. The son’s later recollections describe experiments with bands playing different tunes, quarter-tone instruments and singing in one key against an accompaniment in another. These accounts are filtered through a son’s memory of his father, but the musical questions they pose recur in the scores: how far apart can independent parts move before they stop making a perceptible whole?

Ives was also trained in conventional musicianship. He became a paid church organist as a teenager and wrote the organ Variations on America in 1891. At Yale, from 1894 to 1898, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and large-scale form. His First Symphony belongs to that apprenticeship, with audible debts to European symphonic writing. George died in 1894, shortly after Charles entered Yale. The practical musical culture of Danbury subsequently became both a source of material and a standard against which Ives judged the professional concert world.
composer.epithet: A church organist and insurance executive who made hymns, marching bands and incompatible tempos coexist inside concert music.
